title: The Traceable Brand Score
subtitle: Measures how much of your marketing activity, brand story, and positioning signals are doing revenue-linked work.

questions.text: How was your current brand story developed?

answers.label: We wrote it in a workshop and haven't revisited it since
It came from internal brainstorming about what we wanted to say
We pulled it from client feedback and sales conversations
It was built from specific patterns across multiple client engagements
It came from what clients kept returning to, including the parts they almost skipped because they felt obvious

questions.text: When you describe what you do, where does the explanation start?

answers.label: With our methodology or approach
With the problem we solve in general terms
With a specific type of client outcome
With what the work does in someone's actual day-to-day
With a concrete situation a buyer would immediately recognize as their own

questions.text: If three people on your team each described your brand story right now, how similar would the accounts be?

answers.label: Completely different, no shared language
Similar themes but different words and emphasis
Roughly aligned on the main point
Consistent on the core story, with natural variation in delivery
Aligned on the story and the specific details that make it recognizable

questions.text: When you look at your current brand story, how much of it is assigned a specific job?

answers.label: Most of it is descriptive. It explains what we do.
Parts of it are working. Others feel like context-setting.
The story creates interest but I couldn't tell you exactly what it's changing
Different parts are doing different jobs. I can name most of them.
Every element has a traceable job: positioning, objection handling, proof, or call to action

low.headline: Your story describes what you do. The pipeline work comes next.
low.text: Most brand stories start with what the company wants to say. The ones that move pipeline start with what the buyer keeps coming back to, including the part they almost skip because it feels obvious to them. That's where the brief lives. The work is going back and finding it.
steps: Pull your last five sales or discovery calls and listen for what the client repeated without being prompted.
Write down what they almost skipped over because it felt too obvious. That's often the real differentiator.
Rewrite your opening statement around one of those details rather than around your methodology.

mid.headline: The material is there. Give each piece a job.
mid.text: The Crocs film worked because every choice did a specific job, and that job traced back to what the product actually does in someone's life. Your story has the right material. The next step is assigning each element a role.
steps: List each section of your current brand story and write one sentence on the job it's supposed to do.
For any section without a clear job, cut it or rebuild it around a specific buyer belief you need to shift.
Test the revised version in your next three client conversations and track which parts they respond to.

high.headline: Your story is doing real work. Keep tracing it.
high.text: A story built to do work will keep proving it, or stop proving it, in the numbers. The discipline is continuing to listen for what shifts rather than assuming the brief is permanent.
steps: Audit the story against your last 10 wins: what piece of it showed up in why they chose you?
Identify the element doing the most work and make sure it's the most prominent in your materials.
Set a 6-month review to check whether the story needs updating based on what your buyers are saying.

questions.text: If you asked ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini to describe your company right now, how consistent do you think the answers would be?

answers.label: I haven't checked. I wouldn't know where to start.
I've checked once but don't monitor it
The descriptions are broadly similar but differ on specifics
Mostly consistent. I've identified and addressed a few gaps.
Highly consistent. I know what structural signals drive accurate AI citations of us.

questions.text: When a buyer uses AI to compare you to a competitor before a call, how confident are you in what they find?

answers.label: I have no idea what they find. That's a real gap.
I've thought about it but haven't verified it
I know roughly what AI surfaces but haven't structured content to influence it
I've mapped the key comparison moments and built content for them
Our positioning is structured specifically for the moments buyers use AI to compare options

questions.text: How structured is the public-facing content that AI models learn from?

answers.label: We publish content, but there's no structural intent behind it for AI
We have a content strategy, but AI citation isn't part of how we think about it
We're starting to think about what makes content citable, but haven't made structural changes yet
We've made specific structural choices to improve how AI picks up our positioning
Our content is built so AI models consistently pick up the same positioning language

low.headline: AI is already describing you. The description may be wrong.
low.text: In our research, AI models described the same B2B company in contradictory ways 28% of the time. That gap is structural, and it has a structural fix. The first step is knowing what's actually being said.
steps: Run the same prompt across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini: 'Describe [your company] and what they do for [your buyer type].'
Document every contradiction or gap between the three responses.
Identify the one positioning claim that should appear in all three, then check whether your public content actually supports it.

mid.headline: You know the gap. The next move is structural.
mid.text: Awareness of the problem is a start. AI models cite what is clearly, specifically, and consistently stated in the places they index. The content likely exists. It may just need to do the structural work.
steps: Identify the two or three claims you most need AI to reproduce accurately when buyers compare you.
Check whether those claims appear in consistent language across your website, case studies, and indexed thought leadership.
Make one structural change: rewrite your most-visited page so your core positioning claim appears in a single, unambiguous sentence.

high.headline: You're visible where it counts. Keep tracking it.
high.text: AI models update. What's true today about how they describe you can shift as their training data changes. The discipline is building the audit into a regular process.
steps: Run your AI positioning audit on a quarterly cycle.
Track whether the language AI uses about you is moving toward or away from your intended positioning.
Build a single ground truth page on your site: a structured summary of your positioning that you update when your messaging evolves.

questions.text: When a quarter underperforms, how do you typically categorize what happened?

answers.label: As a failure. Something went wrong and needs fixing.
I look for what broke, but I don't always know whether it was a real setback or something else
I can usually tell the difference between a problem and an investment period, but only after the fact
I can identify in real time whether a slowdown is a step back or a step to the side
I have a clear framework for categorizing performance dips, and I make deliberate choices about which to cut short

questions.text: How often do you make decisions whose return won't show in this quarter's numbers?

answers.label: Rarely. I focus on what moves the needle now.
Occasionally, but I can't always defend them internally
Regularly, though I treat them as a cost rather than an investment
Regularly, and I track them separately from immediate-return activity
It's built into how I plan, with a clear hypothesis for when each will show up in the numbers

questions.text: When you look back at a stretch of months that produced no visible results, what's your honest read?

answers.label: Those periods worry me. Something was wrong.
I assume they were wasted and try not to repeat them
I can sometimes see in hindsight that they set up a later jump
I usually know during those periods whether the work is building toward something
Some of our biggest jumps came after exactly those periods. I've learned not to cut them short.

low.headline: You may be ending investment periods before they pay out.
low.text: A step back and a step to the side look almost identical from the outside. Inside the business, they're completely different. If all underperformance gets the same response, the investments that needed more time get cut.
steps: List the last three periods of flat or declining results and categorize each honestly: was it a problem or an investment?
For each investment period, identify what it was building toward and whether you cut it short.
Set one decision rule before reacting to the next underperformance period: determine which category it falls into first.

mid.headline: You can see it in hindsight. Start seeing it in the moment.
mid.text: Recognizing a step to the side after it's over is useful. Recognizing it while you're in it is what lets you protect those periods rather than react to them.
steps: Before each quarter begins, identify which activities are investments (returns delayed 3-plus months) and which should produce near-term results.
Track these separately so underperformance in one category doesn't trigger cuts in the other.
Review the categorization at 90 days: were your predictions right? Adjust from what you find.

high.headline: You're building with a longer timeline. That's the work.
high.text: Most of the compounding in a business comes from periods that, from the outside, looked like nothing was happening. The discipline is protecting those periods and knowing which ones have earned the protection.
steps: Document the logic behind your current investment-period decisions so they're defensible, not just intuitive.
Share that framework with anyone who has visibility into the numbers, so they're working from the same read.
Set a hypothesis for each current investment period: when should results show, and what would they look like?

questions.text: How much of your current marketing activity can you connect to a pipeline or revenue outcome?

answers.label: Almost none. We measure outputs, not outcomes.
A small portion: a few campaigns where we tracked all the way through
About half: paid and direct channels, but brand and content sit outside it
Most of it. We have attribution across the majority of our programs.
All of it. Every marketing activity has a defined outcome it's responsible for.

questions.text: How do you measure whether your brand story is working?

answers.label: We don't. Brand is treated as unmeasurable.
Engagement metrics: views, likes, shares
Qualitative feedback: whether prospects reference our messaging on calls
Both qualitative and pipeline signals: how often the story affects deal progression
Revenue-linked: we can trace brand story exposure to pipeline entry and close

questions.text: If you removed your brand story from your marketing and kept only your direct-response assets, what do you think would happen to your pipeline?

answers.label: Probably nothing. The brand story isn't doing measurable pipeline work.
It would slow down slightly, but in ways I couldn't prove
I'd lose some inbound, but I'm not sure how much or why
I'd lose specific pipeline I can point to. Brand creates pull that direct response doesn't.
A significant and measurable drop. The brand story is doing traceable pipeline work.

questions.text: Out of every 10 pieces of content your team publishes, how many can you directly connect to a pipeline outcome?
questions.hint: A pipeline outcome means a specific lead, a booked call, or a sale you can trace back to that content. Estimate honestly.

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team spend on brand and content work in total?
questions.hint: Include writing, design, review, approval, and distribution across all channels. Used to estimate your annual cost of untraced marketing work (hours/week x 52 weeks).

questions.text: What is your team's average loaded hourly cost for the people doing this work?
questions.hint: Loaded cost = salary + benefits + overhead per hour. $75 to $150 is a typical range for marketing roles.

low.headline: Most of your marketing is decoration. Decoration has a price tag.
low.text: A story that isn't built to do real work is decoration. People scroll past decoration. The question is what it would take to make each program do a traceable job. For most of your current activity, that answer isn't there yet.
steps: Take your last month of marketing spend, budget and hours combined, and categorize each line item as either 'traceable outcome' or 'no clear link to pipeline.'
For every unlinked activity, name the one job it was supposed to do and whether you can measure it.
Start with one program: redesign it with a single defined outcome and a way to measure it, then run it for 90 days.

mid.headline: You have traceability in patches. Connect them.
mid.text: You've figured out how to trace some of what you do. The gap is that brand and content, the parts of marketing that do the most pipeline work over time, still sit outside that system. That's where the cost is.
steps: Map your buyer journey and identify where brand and content touch it, even if you can't measure it yet.
Choose one brand or content program and write a simple hypothesis: 'If this is working, I'll see X in the pipeline within Y days.'
Run that as a 90-day experiment. The goal is a traceable signal, not perfect attribution.

high.headline: Your marketing is doing traceable work. Hold the standard.
high.text: Most teams stop asking whether their marketing is working once the numbers are moving. The discipline is continuing to trace it, especially for brand and content, where the connection to revenue is the hardest to hold.
steps: Document your current traceability model so it survives team or agency changes.
Add one new program per quarter with a pre-defined outcome and measurement plan before it launches.
Review the full stack annually: which programs have stopped producing traceable outcomes and need to be rebuilt or cut?

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.
